amendments.rule: Rule 67 leaves the head open where a complex frame's carrier is an expressed proper preposition, and that opening is confined to a **contiguous** multiword preposition — *in regard of*, *in furtherance of*, *by reason of*, *in behalf of*. Where the ASV instead **wraps** its phrase in the discontinuous frame *for … sake* and the carrier is a **proper** preposition, the corpus is settled and heads on the prepositional word: `διὰ τὴν ἀλήθειαν` → *for the truth's sake* heads on *for*, as JHN.12.9, JHN.12.30, JHN.14.11, JHN.15.21, REV.2.3 and 2CO.12.10 head *for … sake* and JHN.11.15, JHN.12.30, JHN.17.19 and 2CO.8.9 head *for … sakes* — eleven units against none, only PHP.1.24 hedging. Rule 46 is what decides it and already states the test: the identical English heads on *sake* or *cause* for the postposition `χάριν`, which is the only word carrying the sense there, and on the prepositional word wherever a Greek preposition is expressed. So do not read rule 67's divided case as licensing a head on the frame's supplied noun merely because the frame is complex; what that case divides is where a **contiguous** frame's sense sits, and a discontinuous *for … sake* wrap is not that question. An **improper** preposition is untouched by this and heads on the frame's lexical noun as rule 71 requires. Every unit counted above carries a proper preposition, `διά` or `ὑπέρ`, so none of them is precedent for an adverb governing a case — exactly as rule 95 says of the *by reason of* units that head on *by*, every one of which carries a proper `διά` or `ἐκ`. `ἕνεκεν τῆς βασιλείας τοῦ θεοῦ` → *for the kingdom of God's sake* heads on *sake*, the noun being what renders the adverb's own sense while the *for* belongs to the English idiom rather than answering to the governed case, which is rule 42's reasoning and rule 95's own settlement of `εἵνεκεν` → *by reason of* on *reason*. Decide the class from the lexeme under rule 95 — a preposition governing one case only and forming no verbal compound is improper — and never from the morph tag, which marks `ἕνεκεν` `PREP` exactly as it marks `διά`.
amendments.why: As written, rule 78's second sentence states its holding for the discontinuous *for … sake* wrap without restricting the carrier, and a verse pass applied it to ἕνεκεν at LUK.18.29 against rules 71 and 95. Its own evidence is entirely proper prepositions (διά, ὑπέρ), and rule 95 both classifies ἕνεκεν/εἵνεκεν as improper and heads its complex frame on the frame's noun. The over-broad sentence is the thing to fix, so this replaces rule 78 whole rather than adding a new rule pointing back at it; the eleven-unit holding for a proper preposition is preserved verbatim.

conventions: Where an indefinite τις or τινι stands, it carries the English indefinite determiner and the noun stands bare — Κριτής τις → *a* and *judge* and ἔν τινι πόλει → *a* and *city* at 18:2, *a certain* at 18:9, 18:18 and 18:35 — including where the ASV compresses *a certain* to a bare *a*. Where no indefinite pronoun stands, the supplied determiner is the noun's own rule 51 helper, as χήρα → *a widow* 18:3, Φαρισαῖος → *a Pharisee* 18:10 and ὄχλου → *a multitude* 18:36 have it. Giving the bare *a* to the noun and leaving τις unrepresented is the competing reading and is refused throughout the chapter.

Where the ASV demotes a Greek finite verb to a subordinate English clause and no Greek conjunction stands to introduce it, the supplied introducer is folded onto that verb as a rule 7 helper rather than marked `added` under rule 86: κληρονομήσω → *to inherit* at 18:18, where the ASV promotes the participle ποιήσας to the matrix verb, and ποιήσω → *that I should do* at 18:41, a deliberative subjunctive. Rule 86 is read as scoped to a clause the ASV subordinates whole, not to one whose finite verb it demotes; marking such an introducer `added` remains defensible and both units say so.

ἀναβλέπω heads on *sight* in all three of its units — *I may receive my sight* 18:41, *Receive thy sight* 18:42, *he received his sight* 18:43 — the English being a support-verb rendering whose complement glosses the -βλεπ- root under rules 17 and 91, with the supplied possessive riding along under rules 7 and 11. Its ἀνα- preverb has no separate English particle, so rule 106 splits nothing off. ἐγγίζω heads the same way on the word glossing its own root, *nigh* at 18:35 and *near* at 18:40, and not on the English light verb *drew* or *come*.

report: Cross-verse consistency: no split found. Every recurring construction is analysed one way. The three ἀναβλέπω units (18:41, 18:42, 18:43) all head on *sight*; the two ἐγγίζω units (18:35, 18:40) both head on the ἐγγύς-gloss word; the two ποιέω+ἐκδίκησις pairs (18:7, 18:8) are both collapsed under rule 73 with the source head on the noun, while 18:43's ἔδωκεν αἶνον is split under rule 2 because the ASV spells both elements out; the five supplied junctures *and* (18:11, 18:28, 18:31, 18:33, 18:40) all sit on the finite verb they introduce; the six supplied *when* clauses all sit on their participle; all three articular infinitives (18:1, 18:5, 18:35) give the clause-introducer to the preposition and leave the article unrepresented; every ὁ before a name or before θεός is unrepresented; and 18:13 writes both arms of rule 20 in one verse (τοὺς ὀφθαλμούς → *his*, τὸ στῆθος αὐτοῦ → article empty), which 18:15's τὰ βρέφη → *their* follows.

The rule 106 preverb units differ by that rule's own test rather than uniformly, which is the rule working and not a split: the two εἰσελθεῖν at 18:25 part because the first has no expressed preposition answering to its preverb (*to enter in*) and the second stands beside εἰς (*to enter* / *into*), as 18:24 does.

The candidate table is blind to `added` units, so I read the dump for supplied English. The chapter has exactly one, the appositional *even* at 18:19, which rule 105 makes `added` because an articular appositive follows and no preposition carries it. The other supplied words — *yet* 18:7, *oft* 18:3, *up* 18:21, the four *Do* 18:20, the two *for* 18:25, the objects *it* at 18:15, 18:22, 18:26 and 18:43 — each have a licensing source token, so folding them does not contradict 18:19.

BSB disagreements: all seven are documented convention differences and none is an error. 18:4 καί is rule 65's unwritten intensifier of εἰ καί; 18:7 τῶν and 18:9 τούς are rule 31's second attributive article before a recast participle; 18:14 τόν is rule 20 displaced by αὐτοῦ; 18:16 τῶν is rule 49's article before a substantival demonstrative; 18:34 τό is rule 38 displaced by τοῦτο; 18:37 ὁ is rule 23, the ASV writing *of Nazareth* with no determiner. Nothing was changed to improve the rate.

One correction, at 18:29. ἕνεκεν is an improper preposition — it governs one case only and forms no verbal compound, which is rule 95's own test and rule 95's own worked example — so its discontinuous *for … sake* frame heads on the frame's lexical noun *sake* under rule 71, not on *for*. Rule 78's eleven *for … sake* units all carry a proper preposition (διά or ὑπέρ) and are no precedent for an adverb governing a case, exactly as rule 95 says of the *by reason of* units. Only the target head moves; the unit's tokens are unchanged. Rule 78 is amended so the next verse pass does not read its bare sentence the way this one did.

Three conventions recorded: the indefinite τις taking the English determiner, the supplied introducer on a demoted finite verb (18:18, 18:41), and the ἀναβλέπω/ἐγγίζω heads. One amendment to rule 78; no new rules.
